name: Priya Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers or AI companies. This is confidential. What is a usual workday for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach at the conservatory on Tuesdays, lead a string quartet and record violin parts for studios. I have a master's in music, and I use AI now and then for sorting notes after another player recommends a tool.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What feels secure or uncertain right now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Teaching pays well for this work and my quartet has regular dates; I saved about nine months of expenses. Recording bookings move, but there are plenty of other music jobs nearby.

say: I would welcome **simpler scheduling** while keeping the quartet's live sound central.
I would tell students that **listening** still takes work in rehearsal.
think: My **nine-month reserve** makes a moved studio date manageable.
The **conservatory contract** keeps a quiet recording month from threatening my flat.
do: Keep my **Tuesday classes** and fortnightly quartet concerts this year.
Save **one fifth** of each cleared session fee after paying players and travel.
feel: I feel **calm** about my job and household expenses.
S0.quote: A tidy diary cannot tell a viola when to breathe with a singer.
fieldNote: Her **nine-month reserve** and renewed teaching contract protect her from a single cancelled session.
She accepts **routine help** without expecting a change to concert demand or household pay.

steps.text: Keep Tuesday conservatory classes and fortnightly quartet concerts
Save one fifth of cleared session fees after player and travel costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the string players that a faster diary is useful, but it won't change the concert. Audiences still come to hear our four instruments answer one another.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have nine months of expenses saved and the conservatory has renewed my teaching contract. I still watch the studio diary, because recording dates can move, but a quiet month wouldn't put my flat at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep my Tuesday conservatory classes and the quartet's fortnightly concerts. I will set aside a fifth of each cleared session fee this year, after the players and travel are paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about work and money in this picture. I can enjoy a less cluttered diary without having to remake my living.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened when a session moved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One soundtrack date moved last spring, and the conservatory pay bridged the month. I waited for the revised date rather than take a poor substitute session.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do your students still need from you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my students that a tool may sort parts for us. They still need to hear whether the viola is pushing ahead of the melody. A tidy diary cannot tell a viola when to breathe with a singer.

say: I would price **rehearsal time** separately when clients bring generated scores.
I would ask studios to keep **player fees** visible on every quote.
think: My **arranging fees** could lose a quarter of my income.
Nearby jobs and savings help, but they do not make **lost fees** harmless.
do: Ask **two studios** about generated drafts and record lost offers this term.
Run one **paid clinic** if the conservatory lends a room and twelve players register.
Return **clinic deposits** if fewer than twelve people pay.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a plausible quarter of my income shrinking.
S1.quote: A generated score can save paper, but the rehearsal still takes four people and an afternoon.
fieldNote: She puts a **quarter of earnings** at risk from thinking AI, despite strong savings.
Her **clinic threshold** requires a room and twelve paid places before she expands.

steps.text: Ask two studios how generated drafts change paid arrangements
Run paid ensemble clinic if room and twelve paid places are secured
Return clinic deposits if fewer than twelve players pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the recording team that generated scores will make some small commissions cheaper. I'd ask them to keep paying players for rehearsal time, not bundle it into a flat file fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a quarter of my income comes from arranging and session preparation, so I expect that part to shrink. The conservatory and quartet may hold, and there are plenty of nearby music jobs, but I don't want to spend savings replacing routine fees forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This term I'll ask two studios how they price generated drafts and keep a record of lost arrangement offers. In the first year of this change, I'll teach a paid ensemble clinic only if the conservatory gives me a room and twelve players register.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy when clients send polished mock-ups, but a real quarter of income is at stake. I have time and other employers nearby; I still need to change something. Nine months of savings buys time, not another quarter of income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you charge differently on a generated score?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would quote rehearsal separately from file preparation. A client can bring a draft, but they should know what four players cost for an afternoon. A generated score can save paper, but the rehearsal still takes four people and an afternoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you keep the clinic from losing money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would run one clinic before booking a second. If fewer than twelve pay, I'd return the deposits and continue my normal classes.

say: I would seek **recording rights** and continue booking live concerts through 2028.
I would tell players that **cheap scores** threaten fees before robot performers arrive.
think: **AGI in 2028** could replace arranging and lesson planning before robots arrive around 2031.
My **nine-month reserve** supports a search, but the quarter of pay at risk is real.
do: Separate last year's **three income streams** and seek a two-year teaching renewal now.
Apply to **two nearby schools** after 2028 if arranging fees halve and their terms are sound.
Keep **quartet dates** while seeking replacement ensemble teaching work.
feel: I feel **anxious**, with enough savings to reject a poor contract.
S2.quote: Nine months of savings lets me refuse a bad contract; it doesn't make a lost commission free.
fieldNote: She separates **thinking fees** from live playing and plans around a three-year robot gap.
Her **school applications** depend on lost arranging income and acceptable employment terms.

steps.text: Seek a two-year conservatory teaching renewal
Apply to two nearby schools after 2028 if arranging halves and terms fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my quartet that 2028 is close enough to check our recording contracts now. I would still book concerts, because a system writing music cannot make today's audience disappear by decree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Full AGI in 2028 could do my arranging, marking and lesson planning for less than I charge. Robot players come about 2031, so live performance has a later threat, but the screen work could fall first; nine months of savings makes a transition possible, not painless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll separate last year's teaching, live and arranging pay and seek a two-year teaching renewal. In the first year after 2028, if arrangements fall by half, I'll apply for ensemble teaching at two nearby schools while keeping quartet dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing a part of work I enjoy and a quarter of income. I can make applications without rushing into a bad contract. Nine months of savings lets me refuse a bad contract; it doesn't make a lost commission free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How secure is the conservatory contract?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The conservatory has enough pupils for another year, but a two-year renewal is not promised. I would ask the director before assuming those classes are safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why those two schools rather than any opening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two schools nearby advertise group music posts most summers. I would apply only after seeing the terms, because more hours at worse pay would not solve the loss.

say: I would use **five years** to test paid ensemble coaching.
I would keep the **quartet** performing while school demand becomes clearer.
think: **AGI in 2031** threatens arranging before robot players appear around 2034.
A **coaching module** can replace screen work if enrolment and fees hold.
do: Seek a **six-week module** next term with a written minimum fee.
Move toward **half my income** from teaching and concerts by 2031.
Renew the **module** after AGI only if ten students enrol and its fee holds.
feel: I feel **anxious** about fees shrinking before 2031, though a trial and savings give me room to adjust.
S3.quote: A full room on opening night is not a teaching contract.
fieldNote: The **five-year warning** lets her move pay toward live teaching before AGI.
She requires a **written fee** and repeat enrolment before changing her existing lesson timetable.

steps.text: Seek six-week coaching module with a signed minimum teaching fee
Shift half of income toward teaching and concerts by 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell students that five years is enough to build stronger ensemble teaching, one term at a time. The quartet will keep playing while I learn what audiences and schools will actually pay for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2031 could erase arranging fees, with robot players following around 2034. That gives me time to move income from screen preparation to live coaching, although ordinary software may already take the easiest commissions before 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next term I'll ask the conservatory for a paid chamber coaching module with a written minimum fee. By 2031 I'll try to have half my income from teaching and concerts; in the first year after AGI, I'll renew the module only if at least ten students enrol and the fee remains intact.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about arranging commissions fading before 2031, even with time and savings. I don't assume a school will keep paying just because the first class was enjoyable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge the first module?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would teach a six-week module and collect anonymous feedback after each session. If it works, I can offer it at another nearby school without buying a studio or equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must be signed before you change your teaching week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The minimum fee matters more than a full room on opening night. I'd get the director's signature before moving my existing private pupils around. A full room on opening night is not a teaching contract.

say: I would teach **listening together** while students learn new tools.
I would test a **chamber series** with signed partner costs.
think: At **37**, I will still need earnings when AGI arrives in 2036.
Robot players around **2039** may enter venues, but I have time and savings to test live demand.
do: Get a signed **museum and conservatory plan** before booking the first concert.
Top **savings** back up to nine months from class fees whenever they dip.
Continue the **series** after 2036 only if tickets cover players and insurance.
feel: I feel **calm** about my home, with some doubt about future venues.
S4.quote: If ticket sales only pay for posters, we stop, even if the audience claps.
fieldNote: Her **strong reserve** and nearby work keep the long-run threat from becoming an immediate crisis.
She makes the **series conditional** on signed costs and ticket sales covering players and insurance.

steps.text: Get signed museum and conservatory fee and room plan before booking
Top savings back to nine months from paid class fees if they dip
Continue chamber series after 2036 if tickets cover players and insurance

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my students a decade is a long time to learn new instruments and ways of working. I would still ask them to listen across the quartet, rather than chase a perfect file.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 37 in 2036, I will need work for years beyond full AGI, and robot performers around 2039 may enter some venues. Ten years lets me build a teaching post and a live series, while the arranging fees could thin out much sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll ask the conservatory and museum for a joint chamber series if both sign a fee and room plan. Across the decade I'll top savings back up to nine months from class fees whenever they dip; in the first year after 2036, I'll continue the series only if ticket sales still cover musicians and insurance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel cautiously calm about my household, though I do not know what live audiences will choose in ten years. The cushion gives me time to stop a failing series without losing my home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What cost could stop the first concert?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The museum has a small hall but charges for evening staff. I would get the cost in writing and cancel the first date if the two partners cannot cover it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you end the series?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want a series that pays the players before I draw a fee. If ticket sales only pay for posters, we stop, even if the audience claps.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because arranging fees could halve before I can move enough teaching work into place. A two-year conservatory renewal and fair recording terms would give me time to choose good contracts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether listeners can tell a responsive quartet from a flawless generated file. I think many can, but I'd rather test ticket sales than make that a slogan.

headlineQuote: Nine months of savings buys time, not another quarter of income.
portrait: Priya is a **27-year-old** violinist with a music master's degree, leading a quartet, teaching and recording studio parts.
She has **high pay**, nine months of savings and many nearby music jobs, so ordinary cancellations are manageable.
She sees **arranging and lesson planning** exposed to thinking AI before robot performers arrive three years after AGI.
She tests **ensemble teaching and concerts** with signed fees, room terms, enrolment and ticket conditions.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because arranging income could fall before enough teaching work replaces it.
whatWouldHelp: A **two-year conservatory renewal** and fair recording terms would let her choose sound replacement contracts.
